hero.name: Swati
hero.who: a 27-year-old railway booking clerk in Siliguri who wants to write stories but freezes

story.b: Swati works the booking counter at a railway station in Siliguri from seven in the morning till three. She has a story in her head that will not leave: a girl from a tea garden who dreams of running her own roadside dhaba. Every night, in her rented room near Hill Cart Road, she opens a fresh notebook. She writes one line, crosses it out, writes another and tears out the page. After two hours she has a single paragraph she hates. Then she scrolls through posts by young writers who seem to produce pages effortlessly. She has been about to start this story for three years. Some nights she wonders if real writers are simply born different.

ask.q: Swati has been about to start writing for three years. What would help her most?
o: Wait for a burst of inspiration on a quiet holiday
Buy a writing course and finish it before writing anything
Accept that writers improve by reading and writing regularly, and begin small
ask.why: Inspiration rarely arrives on schedule, and a course can become one more reason to delay. Writers improve the plain way, by reading a lot and writing regularly, even when it feels bad. Beginning small removes the pressure of the blank page.

chapters.take: Writing gets easier by writing, not by waiting to feel ready.

story.b: Swati makes two simple rules. First, she always carries a book. She reads in the slow hour at the counter after the morning rush, in the shared auto home, while waiting for her rice to cook. Bengali novels, English short stories, even a terrible thriller from the station bookstall. The bad one teaches her a lot. She notices how its characters all sound the same and how nothing feels real. Second, she writes one page every night before dinner, however she feels. Many pages are clumsy. Some are embarrassing. But after a month she has thirty pages, and the tea garden girl has a name, Mitali, and a stubborn little brother.

ask.q: Swati's friend wants to write but says she has no time to read. What advice fits best?
o: Skip reading and focus only on writing
Read in small gaps, like commutes, and write a set amount daily
Read only great classics so bad writing does not rub off
ask.why: Reading shows what works and what fails, so skipping it starves the writing. Reading only classics misses the lessons even weak books can teach. Small daily reading in spare moments, plus a steady writing amount, builds skill through sheer volume.

chapters.take: Read in every spare moment, and write a set amount every day.

story.b: On Sunday, Swati reads her thirty pages from the start. She winces. Mitali was extremely tired. The sky was incredibly beautiful. Her brother spoke very angrily. Mitali commenced her journey. Every sentence seems to lean on an extra word to hold it up. So Swati goes through with a pencil. Extremely tired becomes Mitali sat down on the bus step and did not get up. The incredibly beautiful sky becomes the hills went pink behind the tea bushes. Commenced becomes began. Spoke very angrily becomes snapped. The pages get shorter and lighter. When she reads them aloud in her room, they sound more like a real person talking and less like an exam essay.

ask.q: Swati's sentence reads: The man was very, very tired after the extremely long journey. How could she improve it?
o: Use plain, vivid words, like: The man stumbled off the night bus
Add more describing words so readers feel the tiredness
Use grander vocabulary so it sounds more literary
ask.why: Piling up words like very and extremely props up weak writing rather than fixing it, and fancy words often sound stiff. A plain, concrete verb and image does the work by itself, showing the tiredness instead of announcing it.

chapters.take: Choose the plain, strong word over the fancy or padded one.

story.b: Swati's roommate, a nurse she calls Didi, sees the notebook and asks to read it. Swati hesitates. Two years ago she showed a half-finished story to her cousin, who said kindly that it was a bit slow. Swati never touched that story again. So this time she smiles and says not yet, but soon. She keeps writing the first draft only for herself, following Mitali wherever she goes, not worrying about what anyone will think. Six weeks later the draft is finished, rough but whole. Only then does she give it to Didi and to an old school friend who reads a lot. She asks them where they got bored and what confused them.

ask.q: Halfway through her first draft, Swati's roommate asks to read it. What should Swati do?
o: Share it right away, since early feedback saves time
Share it, but only the best parts
Politely wait until the full draft is done, then share and revise with readers in mind
ask.why: Early opinions, even kind ones, can crush a fragile draft before its shape is clear, and showing only the best parts still invites outside voices too soon. Finishing privately lets the story find itself, and feedback afterwards helps her revise it for readers.

chapters.take: Write the first draft for yourself. Revise the next one for your readers.

story.b: With her readers' notes in hand, Swati puts the story in a drawer and leaves it there through Durga Puja. For three weeks she visits pandals with her family and does not read a word of it. When she opens the drawer again, she sees the story with new eyes. The opening has two whole pages describing the hills before anything happens. A long paragraph about a stray dog, her favourite paragraph, does nothing for Mitali at all. Swati takes a deep breath and cuts. She copies the dog paragraph into a separate file, so it is not lost forever. The story is now shorter, faster and far more alive.

ask.q: Swati loves a beautiful paragraph that does nothing for her story. What should she do?
o: Keep it, since good writing should never be thrown away
Cut it from the story and save it in a separate file if she likes
Rewrite the story around it so that it fits
ask.why: A paragraph that does not serve the story slows readers down, however lovely it is. Bending the story to fit it puts one passage above the whole piece. Cutting it, and saving it elsewhere if that softens the loss, makes the story tighter.

chapters.take: Revise by cutting what does not serve the piece, even lines you love.

story.b: For her next story, Swati wants to plan every twist in advance. She fills two pages with arrows and boxes, then feels the story go stiff and dead. So she tries something else. She starts with only a situation. An old tea taster and a runaway schoolboy are stuck together at a level crossing near Sevoke because a goods train has broken down. The wait might be four hours. That is all she knows. She writes what they would honestly say and do. The boy lies about where he is going. The old man notices his school badge but says nothing. Swati has no idea what happens next, and she cannot wait to find out.

ask.q: Swati wants to plan every twist of her next story before writing a word. What might work better?
o: Start with an interesting situation and real characters, then see what they do
Copy the plot structure of a bestselling thriller
Write the ending first and force the story toward it
ask.why: Heavy plotting can make characters feel like puppets pushed toward fixed twists, and borrowing someone else's plot or forcing an ending does the same. Starting with a strong situation and honest characters lets the story unfold naturally, which often makes it feel alive.

chapters.take: Put real characters in a tricky situation and let them show you the story.

story.b: In the spring, a small online magazine for new writers from the Northeast and North Bengal accepts the story about Mitali. Swati reads the acceptance email at the booking counter between two passengers and has to go and stand on the platform for a minute. She still works her shift. She still reads in the slow hour and in the shared auto. She still writes one page every night before dinner, even when it is bad. The story of the tea taster and the runaway boy is now forty pages long, and it keeps surprising her. Didi reads each draft only when Swati says it is ready. The stray dog paragraph is waiting for its own story.

chapters.take: Daily reading, plain words and honest revision turned a frozen writer into a working one.
